title: Neora Valley and Red Pandas: An Honest Guide
meta_description: Neora Valley National Park from Lava: permits, guides, fees, the Mouchuki camp, the monsoon closure, birding, and your real chances of seeing a red panda.
summary: Neora Valley National Park, set up in 1986, climbs from 183 m to about 3,200 m east of Lava. You enter from Lava with a forest permit and a registered guide, paying about ₹150–300 a person plus ₹600–1,000 for the guide. Red pandas live here, but sightings are rare: come for the forest and the birds.

sections.heading: What Neora Valley is
paras: Neora Valley National Park was declared in 1986 and covers the catchment of the Neora river east of Lava, in the Kalimpong district of West Bengal. Few parks in the region climb so far: the lowest edge sits at about 183 m in the Dooars plains near Samsing, and the highest point, Rachela Danda, rises to about 3,150 m on the ridge where West Bengal meets Sikkim and Bhutan. The park borders Sikkim to the north and the Samtse district of Bhutan to the east, so animals move freely across three administrations.

That 3,000 m climb packs several forests into one valley: warm broadleaf woods near the plains, then oak and rhododendron through the middle, and bamboo thickets under mossy trees near the top. The Neora river that drains it is Kalimpong town's main water source, so the forest here matters well beyond the park boundary. For visitors, the upper park is reached only on foot with a forest guide, and only in the dry months.

sections.heading: The animals, and the honest odds
paras: Neora Valley is best known for the red panda, the small rust-red climber of bamboo and oak forest. The park also holds clouded leopard, Himalayan black bear and the satyr tragopan, a crimson pheasant with blue facial skin that is heard calling far more often than it is seen. These are real residents, and the forest department protects the park largely for them.

We will be straight with you: on a normal day visit, your chance of seeing a red panda is low, and most visitors never see one. Red pandas spend much of the day high in trees, are most active around dawn and dusk, and live mainly in the upper forest that a short visit barely touches. Clouded leopards are nocturnal and very rarely seen by anyone. What you will almost certainly get is the forest itself, mixed flocks of small birds, fresh pug marks or scats your guide can read, and the sound of barking deer. Anyone who promises a red panda is selling something.

sections.heading: Getting in from Lava: permits and guides
paras: The usual way in is from Lava, about 30–34 km from Kalimpong via Algarah. As we understand the current rule, you need a forest entry permit from the Lava range office and must go with a registered local guide; a vehicle fee applies if you drive to the park gate. Expect roughly ₹150–300 a person for entry, ₹600–1,000 a day for the guide, plus the vehicle fee. Rules, fees and the number of permits issued each day change, so check current status before you travel.

Carry a photo ID for every person; foreign nationals should carry their passports. Go to the range office the evening before or at opening time, because the best hours inside are the early ones and a late start means you walk in the midday lull. Your homestay in Lava, Kolakham or Rishyap can usually connect you with a guide and a car the night before. A reserved car from Kalimpong to Lava costs ₹2,500–3,000 one way; shared jeeps are ₹120–180 a seat but few, and mostly leave in the morning.

A typical day for our travellers looks like this: tea at 5.30 am, the range office as it opens, a drive toward the park gate, then 3–5 hours on foot with the guide, turning back by early afternoon when cloud usually fills the valley. Budget about ₹3,000–4,500 for two people for the day, covering entry, guide, vehicle and car hire from Lava, before food. Pack lunch from your homestay the night before. If you have two days, spend the second on the village lanes around Kolakham or Rishyap rather than a second park visit: the birds are often better and it costs nothing.

sections.heading: The Dooars side: Mouchuki camp
paras: The park has a second, lower doorway. WBFDC runs the Mouchuki camp on the Samsing side, in the Dooars below the southern edge of the park, where the forest is warmer, lower and wetter than at Lava. It suits travellers combining Neora Valley with Gorumara or the tea gardens of the Dooars, and it is a different experience from the Lava side: river valleys and broadleaf forest rather than high bamboo. Rates, availability and trail access at Mouchuki are set by WBFDC and the forest department; check current status before you travel.
Plan the upper and lower parts of Neora Valley as separate visits. They are reached by separate roads, hours apart by car, and most travellers choose one or the other on a single trip.

sections.heading: When to go, and the monsoon closure
paras: The park closes for the monsoon, usually from mid-June to mid-September, when rain, landslides and leeches make the trails unsafe and wildlife breeds undisturbed. The closure dates are set each year; check current status before you travel.

October to December is the clearest time: dry trails, cold mornings at 2,000 m and above, and Kanchenjunga visible from the Lava and Rishyap ridges. March to May brings rhododendron flowers, singing birds and tragopans calling, at the cost of afternoon haze and the first pre-monsoon showers. January and February are cold, sometimes with snow on the upper ridges, and quiet. Whatever the month, aim to be at the park gate by 7 am.

sections.heading: Birding around Lava, Kolakham and Rishyap
paras: You do not need to be inside the park to see good birds. The forest edges around Lava, the 4 km path from Lava up to Rishyap, and the lanes of Kolakham all sit at 1,980–2,590 m, the same band as the park's middle forest. Walk them slowly between 6 and 9 am, when mixed flocks move through the trees, and you will see more than in a hurried park visit. These are the birds we would expect a patient beginner to find on a two-day stay:
list: Blue whistling thrush, loud at dawn by every stream and drain
Verditer flycatcher, a turquoise bird on open perches along the road
Great barbet, heard long before it is seen, calling from tall trees
Rufous sibia and several laughingthrushes, in noisy parties through the undergrowth
Green-tailed and other sunbirds at flowering shrubs in March and April
Kalij pheasant, crossing quiet forest roads early in the morning
Woodpeckers and minivets in the mixed flocks of the oak forest

sections.heading: What to carry and how to behave
paras: Neora Valley is a forest with few facilities. Pack for a full day on foot and leave nothing behind.
list: Leech socks or long socks over trousers, and salt or a lighter to remove leeches safely, from May to October
A rain shell, a warm layer and a cap: under the trees it is several degrees colder than in the sun at Lava
Binoculars, ideally 8x or 10x; the canopy is high and dense
Water, lunch and snacks for the whole day; there is nothing to buy inside
Stay with your guide, keep voices low, and never play bird calls from a phone to draw birds out
Carry every wrapper and bottle back to Lava

faqs.q: Can you see red pandas in Neora Valley National Park?
faqs.a: Red pandas live in Neora Valley, but the chance of seeing one on a normal day visit is low, and most visitors never do. They are shy, spend much of the day high in trees, and live mainly in the upper bamboo and oak forest. Go early with a registered guide, walk quietly, and treat a sighting as a rare bonus rather than the point of the trip.

faqs.q: How do we get a permit for Neora Valley?
faqs.a: As we understand the current rule, permits are issued at the Lava range office, and you must enter with a registered local guide. Bring photo ID for everyone, and passports for foreign nationals. Expect about ₹150–300 a person for entry, ₹600–1,000 a day for the guide, and a vehicle fee. Rules and fees change; check current status before you travel.

The park usually closes for the monsoon from mid-June to mid-September, for safety and to protect breeding wildlife. The exact closing and opening dates are announced each year by the forest department, and landslides on the Lava road can close access at other times too. Check current status before you travel, especially in early June and late September.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Neora Valley?
faqs.a: October to December gives dry trails, clear skies and cold mornings, and is the best time for most visitors. March to May is better for birds and rhododendron flowers, with more haze and the first showers. January and February are cold and quiet, sometimes with snow on the upper ridges. Avoid the monsoon months, when the park is closed.

faqs.q: How far is Neora Valley from Kalimpong?
faqs.a: Lava, the usual entry point, is about 30–34 km from Kalimpong via Algarah, around 1.5–2 hours by car. A reserved car costs about ₹2,500–3,000 one way, and shared jeeps from the Kalimpong motor stand cost ₹120–180 a seat but are few and mostly leave in the morning. From Lava a short drive takes you toward the park gate.

faqs.q: What is the Mouchuki camp in Neora Valley?
faqs.a: Mouchuki is a WBFDC camp on the Samsing side of Neora Valley, in the Dooars below the park's southern edge. It gives access to the lower, warmer forest and suits travellers combining Neora Valley with Gorumara or the Dooars tea gardens. Rates and trail access are set by WBFDC and the forest department; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Do we need a guide for Neora Valley?
faqs.a: Yes. Entry from Lava is with a registered local guide, at about ₹600–1,000 a day. A good guide is also the difference between a walk through green forest and a real wildlife morning: they know where birds feed, read tracks and scats, and keep you on safe trails. Your homestay in Lava, Kolakham or Rishyap can usually arrange one the night before.

faqs.q: Where should we stay for Neora Valley?
faqs.a: Lava is the practical base, with the WBFDC Lava Eco Tourism Centre at about ₹2,000–3,000 a room and village homestays around ₹1,500–2,200 a person with meals. Kolakham, 8 km beyond Lava on the park edge, and Rishyap, 10 km by road, are quieter homestay villages with Kanchenjunga views and good birding on their doorsteps.

faqs.q: Are there leeches in Neora Valley?
faqs.a: Yes, from about May to October leeches are on every trail and road edge, and they are worst just before and after the monsoon closure. They are harmless but unpleasant. Wear leech socks or tuck trousers into long socks, check your ankles every half hour, and remove them with salt or a little heat rather than pulling. Dry winter months are almost leech-free.
